note:
This section serves as the first part of an introduction to Judges, and in it the gradual shift from conquest to coexistence comes to expression. Additionally, the need for leaders who will fight against the Canaanites is expressed in the opening verse of the book. The covenant-keeping successes and failures of the various tribes, and God’s judgment on Israel for the covenant failure of letting the Canaanites live in the land, are recounted (cf. Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). The space and detail given to Judah’s successes (vv. 3–20) contrast strongly with the brief accounts of the failures of the other tribes (vv. 21–36). The house of Joseph is treated positively (vv. 22–26), but Judah’s prominence is evidence that Israel should look to that tribe for leadership.

**1:1–8** This opening story demonstrates that the land was conquered in principle under Joshua, yet there remain both pockets of Canaanite resistance (cf. Josh. 13:1) and large areas that still need to be settled. The allotted territory generally belongs to Israel, but many of the original inhabitants need to be dislodged.

**1:1 After the death of Joshua.** The book of Joshua opens similarly: “After the death of Moses” (Josh. 1:1).

**Who.** The Israelites ask an almost identical question at the end of the book: “Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?” (20:18). A question raised at the beginning of the book to initiate holy war against the Canaanites is raised near the end of the book to initiate holy war within Israel.

**Canaanites.** The Canaanites are one of several groups inhabiting the land of Canaan. The Israelites have been commanded to dispossess and destroy them (Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). Whether the Israelites can obey these terms of the covenant will be the issue for this entire introductory section.

God’s choice is Judah. David and his heirs will come from this tribe, and this serves as evidence for God’s choice of the house of David during the war between the house of David and the house of Saul.

verse_quote: cut off his thumbs and his big toes.
note: The severing of the digits of Adoni-bezek is a form of ironic justice: he committed this act against seventy kings, and now it is done to him. It is a symbol of taking away one’s power and authority.
Judah obeys the covenant by destroying the inhabitants without mercy (Deut. 7:1–2; 20:16–20). Judah does not occupy Jerusalem at this point (v. 21).
These verses, describing the victories of Caleb and Othniel, are essentially the same as Josh. 15:15–19.
Caleb, though of Kenizzite ancestry (Gen. 15:19; Num. 32:12), is counted as belonging to the tribe of Judah. He represented Judah when the spies were sent into Canaan (Num. 13:6).

He is the first judge whose judgeship is recounted in the book (3:7–11).

**Achsah.** It is significant that Othniel, the first and best of the judges, is married to the daughter of the godly Caleb, one of two (Joshua being the other) from the wilderness generation to enter the Promised Land. The significance is seen in connection with the theme of intermarriage to pagan women as the problem that leads eventually to apostasy (3:5–6). Othniel represents the solution, not the problem; in contrast, Samson is the epitome of the problem (14:1; 16:1; 16:4).

LORD **was with Judah.** God keeps His covenant promise (v. 2). With the exception of the house of Joseph, the writer deals briefly with the rest of the tribes, describing the failures of their efforts at settlement (1:27–36 note). Although the Ephraimites considered themselves to be the leading tribe among the Israelites, the book of Judges points to the ever-increasing role played by Judah, as was promised in Jacob’s blessing to Judah in Gen. 49:8.

**chariots of iron.** Such chariots, with their wooden wheels overlaid with iron, were powerful weapons, especially on the level plains. According to archaeological site surveys of the land, the major concentration of Canaanite settlements was in the valleys and plains of Canaan. In Iron Age I (c. 1200 B.C..), settlement surveys have demonstrated a great increase of sites in the hill country.
Caleb, from the tribe of Judah, is an example of faithfulness to the covenant. In Deut. 1:36–37, Caleb is rewarded for his covenant obedience, which flows from faith in God’s promise.

The writer specifies that Benjamin, Saul’s tribe, does not make a final conquest of Jerusalem. This contrasts with the victories of Judah and provides an argument for Israel not to side with the house of Saul during the war between the house of David and the house of Saul.
LORD **was with them.** Besides Judah (v. 19), only with regard to the house of Joseph is it said that “the LORD was with them.”
Judah, Benjamin, and Joseph have already been mentioned. The shortcomings of the remaining tribes are briefly presented in outline fashion.
See chs. 17, 18.

This passage reviews the preceding chapter and, like 2:20–3:6, provides the background for the narrative that follows. The covenant was made between God and “your fathers,” and the covenant terms forbid treaties or mixed worship with the Canaanites. Failure to observe these requirements brings the judgment of the covenant on Israel (Deut. 28–31).

**2:1 the angel of the** LORD**.** Because the words of God’s preeminent messenger are the words of the Lord Himself (6:11–24; cf. Ex. 3:1–17), this should likely be read as a theophany, that is, a visible revelation of God. See 6:11–24; 13:2–23. The angel of the Lord led Israel out of captivity in Egypt and fought for them (Ex. 14:19; 23:20–23; 33:2; Num. 20:16; Is. 63:9). Some commentators suggest that the angel of the Lord, at least in these cases, is a preincarnate appearance of the Messiah.

**Gilgal.** At this time, the ark of the covenant is at Gilgal (Josh. 5:1–12).

**I brought you up from Egypt.** The Ten Commandments begin with the same statement (Ex. 20:2; Deut. 5:6), a reminder that the history of what God has done is linked to His commands. The sovereign God who sets out the terms of the covenant identifies Himself as the benefactor of His people.

**and brought you into the land that I swore.** God has kept His oath (Josh. 23:3–16). The chief difference here between God and His people is that God keeps His vow while the people break theirs.

**I will never break my covenant.** See Deut. 7:9.

verse_quote: you shall break down their altars.
note:
Idolatry is the leading, typical act of covenant breaking (v. 11; Ex. 34:13; Num. 33:52; Deut. 7:5; 12:3; Josh. 23:16).

**you have not obeyed.** Israel has contracted marriages with the people of the land (3:5–6) and has not torn down their altars (6:25–32). The Canaanites cannot be driven out because of Israel’s sin.

Intermarriage and all other relationships with the Canaanites have been forbidden because such contact will lead to idolatry (Ex. 23:33; 34:12; Num. 33:55; Deut. 7:16; Josh. 23:12–13). For disobeying the terms of the covenant, Israel will suffer what Canaan suffered: removal from the land (Num. 33:56; Josh. 23:13; 2 Kin. 17:5–8; 25:1–11).

This section serves as the second part of an introduction to Judges, and in it the gradual shift from Israel’s mere coexistence alongside the Canaanites to Israel’s apostate embrace of Canaanite religion comes to expression.

**2:6–10** This section, except for v. 10, is similar to Josh. 24:28–31 and introduces the pattern for the cycle of the judges that follows.
LORD**.** Echoes Josh. 24:31. Covenant obedience led to blessing in the land for Joshua’s generation.

LORD **or the work that he had done for Israel.** One generation is to declare God’s wonders to the next (Deut. 4:9; 6:1–6). Later psalmists extol them (Pss. 44:1–3; 78:2–8). If God’s people know Him personally and what He has done, they will obey the commands of His covenant. But after Joshua, the leaders—heads of families, priests, and judges—fail to keep the covenant or to tell the next generation about God’s mighty deeds.

This passage presents the macrostructure or pattern of Israel’s history during the period of the judges. The first part of the sketch is Israel’s apostasy (vv. 11–13). It is followed by God’s response of anger and judgment by giving Israel into the hands of her enemies (vv. 14, 15). Subsequently, the Lord raises up a judge to deliver the people (v. 16). Although the judge succeeds for a time, the nation quickly returns to its ways of apostasy (v. 17). The nation reverts to wickedness, and the people become more corrupt than the previous generation (vv. 18, 19). The period of the judges is a downward spiral. See Introduction.

**2:11 did what was evil.** Lit. “the evil”; the definite article refers specifically to the sin of apostasy. This refrain occurs at 2:11; 3:7, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 10:6; 13:1.

**served the Baals.** Israel’s evil is summed up in their worship of false gods (v. 2 note). They choose Baal, the Canaanite storm god, and reject the Lord, who brought them through the Red Sea and is the true Lord of the storm. “Baals” is plural because Baal is worshiped differently in various Canaanite localities. Thus, “Baal” contrasts with the Lord, who is one who has integrity of character and is the same wherever and whenever He is encountered (Deut. 6:4; Heb. 13:8).
These are the goddesses of fertility in the Canaanite pantheon.

See Deut. 28:48; 1 Sam. 12:9. Israel’s enemies and oppressors have no power over God’s people unless God allows it. Israel’s conquest is now reversed, as people from outside Canaan (Arameans, Moabites, Midianites, Amalekites, and Philistines) oppress the Israelites, the new inhabitants of the land (3:8–12; 4:2; 6:1; 10:7; 13:1).

LORD **was against them.** The hand of the Lord is associated with the saving power of God (Ex. 3:20; 6:1; 13:3; Deut. 4:34). Now the same hand is turned against them in punishment. The Lord is faithful both to bless and to judge. When God rescues His people, He rescues them from their enemies as an act of grace. It is His own judgment that allows their enemies to prevail, and in rescuing them He must turn His own judgment aside.

The term for “judge” is not used in the sense of one who decides court cases but of one who delivers from injustice and oppression. The primary task of a judge is military in nature. The bulk of the material in the cycle of judges focuses on the military deliverance of the judges.
Since the covenant agreement can be compared to marriage, harlotry is a standard metaphor for faithlessness and disobedience (8:33; Deut. 31:16; Hosea).
The people’s groaning moves their God (Ex. 2:24; 6:5).

Neither their judges (v. 17) nor the memory of how they have been delivered is enough to make the people keep the covenant (v. 10).

**stubborn.** This is one of the words used in Exodus regarding Pharaoh’s hard heart. He adamantly refused to allow Israel to leave Egypt; Israel now displays a similar obstinacy in her apostasy.

Explains why there are still Canaanites during a period when Israel was faithful (vv. 6–9; cf. Deut. 7:22–23; Josh. 13:1–7). Verses 20–22 and 3:1–4 provide a new reason for God’s leaving the Canaanites: to test the hearts of the people.

See 2:10. Even God’s judgment is not without grace. The testing is an opportunity for a generation who has not seen the Lord work on their behalf to exercise faith and see His might with their own eyes (v. 2).
The Canaanites and the Hivites are to be utterly destroyed (Deut. 7:1, 2).
All these are nations devoted to destruction (3:3 note). Israel violates the covenant by living among them and not destroying them.

This coexistence leads the Israelites into the apostasy of idolatry. The result of making covenants with the Canaanites rather than destroying that population is repeatedly explained in the following narrative cycles (2:2). It becomes clear that the people care more about covenants with their pagan neighbors than about their covenant with God.
See 2:11, 13 and notes. This is the apostasy that results from the coexistence mentioned in v. 6.

See notes on 1:13. Othniel is the epitome of a godly judge, being married to the godly Achsah. He forms a sharp contrast with Samson, seen in his relations with foreign women (14:1; 16:1; 16:4); see Introduction: Literary Features. In this account the prominence of Judah in Israel is highlighted, since the first judge is from Judah and is the only judge without an explicit failure in his covenant keeping. The success of Judah anticipates the future enthronement of David, who comes from that tribe.

LORD**.** The Spirit is also mentioned in connection with Gideon, Jeph­thah, and Samson. By the gift of the Spirit, the judge is empowered to deliver the people (6:34; 11:29; 13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). This idiom does not necessarily reflect spiritual regeneration, but it signifies a special dispensation of the Lord’s power and authority granted to the judge. The Spirit of God temporarily empowers the judge to perform extraordinary feats of deliverance.

**he judged Israel.** This means he fights for Israel and delivers the nation. See Introduction: Title.

verse_quote: the land had rest forty years.
note: Though the pattern in 2:11–19 does not mention the time length of peace, the stories themselves end with a comment about peace or the lack of it (v. 30; 5:31; 8:28; 12:7; 15:20; 16:31).

The story of Ehud humiliates the oppressor of God’s people.

**3:12** See note on 2:11.

**Eglon the king of Moab.** The Lord strengthens the pagan king to be used as His instrument of judgment.

Old enemies from the exodus period (Num. 14:45; 21:24).

**the city of palms.** The city of Jericho in the Jordan Valley; it was the first site conquered by Israel during the period of the conquest (Josh. 6).

Lit. “with his right hand restricted.” This is not the usual Hebrew word for “left-handed.” It is used elsewhere only in 20:16, also for the men of Benjamin. “Benjamin” can be translated “son of the right hand,” and the writer may be making a pun about a left-handed son of the right hand.
Lit. “two mouths.” The sword of Ehud is double-edged.
The Hebrew term for “message” is “word” or “thing.” Perhaps a double entendre in which Eglon believes Ehud had a secret word, when in fact Ehud has a secret thing, a sword, in his cloak.

verse_quote: I have a message from God for you.
note: The secret message of v. 19 becomes a divine message. It is not a false word but the true word of God working against the same rod raised up by God to punish His people (v. 12 note). Eglon has been useful as a tool of God’s wrath against Israel, but now that wrath comes back upon him. Ehud does not invoke the covenantal name of Yahweh but rather employs the generic name Elohim.

LORD **has given.** Each major judge except for Othniel verbally acknowledges God’s control in Israel’s victory (4:14; 7:15; 11:21–30; 15:18; 16:28).

**the fords of the Jordan.** This seizure results in the conquest of Canaanites, whereas the corresponding seizure in 12:5 results in the conquest of Israelites. See Introduction: Literary Features. Holy war against Canaan later gives way to civil war within Israel, owing to Israel’s apostasy.
See note on v. 11.

Shamgar is mentioned only here and in the song of Deborah (5:6). Since Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war, perhaps “son of Anath” was a war hero’s nickname. Alternatively, Anath could be a place name (see 1:33 for mention of Beth-anath).

**600 ... with an oxgoad.** Samson later slays one thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey (15:15–17).

Perhaps a descendant of the Jabin mentioned in Josh. 11:1–9.

**Hazor.** During the northern campaign under Joshua, Israel had destroyed this city (Josh. 11:10–13). Apparently, the Canaanites recaptured and resettled the site, and it had become a royal center in Canaan.

The same verb is used of Israel’s circumstances in Egypt (Ex. 22:21).

**twenty years.** The first oppression lasted eight years (3:8) and the second for eighteen years (3:14), but this one under Jabin lasts two decades. There is an intensification in Israel’s sin and its oppression.

verse_quote: Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth.
note: Lit. “a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth.” This emphasizes that this woman is the leader in Israel, and this is because the men lack faith, courage, and leadership (vv. 8, 9 notes). Deborah, a prophetess, is introduced at the point where the narrator usually mentions the deliverer (6:8 note). The word “prophetess” occurs five times in the OT (Ex. 15:20; 2 Kin. 22:14; 2 Chron. 34:22; Neh. 6:14; Is. 8:3). Although there is a feminine ending on the word “prophet,” the author adds the word “woman” in his description. He is underscoring the unique, special character of this judgeship.
That is, she is a magistrate, handing down legal decisions.
A rounded hillock standing isolated on the north side of the plain in the Jezreel Valley, approximately fourteen miles (22 km) southwest of the Sea of Galilee.
The River Kishon is near the base of Mount Tabor and is virtually dry for much of the year (v. 15 note).

Barak is asking Deborah to risk her life to verify the truth of her words, and he is also asking a woman to do what he had been assigned to do. From his point of view, the mission is suicidal, since the exposed Mount Tabor can easily be surrounded by the chariots of Sisera, cutting off any escape. Barak’s faith is not equal to this danger.

verse_quote: will not lead to your glory.
note:
Barak is punished for doubting (v. 8). Deborah has spoken the word of God to him (v. 6), yet he hesitates to obey. He refuses to go unless Deborah accompanies him.

**for the** LORD **will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.** The enemy will not be delivered to Barak but to a woman. Jael (v. 17) will succeed where faithless Barak will fail (vv. 18–22). The male leaders in Israel are shamed for their lack of courage and leadership.
See 5:13–18. These are the two tribes located directly north of the Jezreel Valley and Mount Tabor.
See note on v. 7.
LORD **has given Sisera.** Deborah confirms her word from the Lord (v. 7). It is the Lord who fights for Israel.
LORD **routed.** From Deborah’s song we learn that the Lord does this by sending rain that causes flash floods, trapping the chariots (5:4).
See 5:24–27 for the poetic account.

verse_quote: drove the peg into his temple.
note: No motive is given for Jael’s action. A woman kills Sisera by striking his head, and the Lord’s word to Barak is fulfilled (v. 9). In this era, women are not normally warriors, and it is considered shameful to die at the hands of a woman (9:53–54). Jael drives the point home that Israel is saved by the hand of a woman. In the corresponding story about Abimelech, a woman crushes the head of Abimelech by dropping a millstone on him (9:53); see Introduction: Literary Features.

The song of Deborah and Barak is a victory song celebrating what has just taken place (cf. Ex. 15:1–18, the song of Moses). Scholars acknowledge that its structure, grammar, and vocabulary reflect an early date. The song is also recognized for its outstanding literary quality.

verse_quote: That the leaders took the lead.
note: Leadership is a major theme in Judges.

verse_quote: from Seir ... from the region of Edom.
note:
Mount Seir is the main mountain ridge running through Edom, Israel’s point of departure for the battles of conquest (Deut. 33:2). God is pictured as the mighty warrior going before His people.

**5:4, 5 the earth trembled ... before the** LORD **.** God is pictured as a warrior who fights by means of the created elements.

**earth ... heavens.** A literary feature called a _merism_, which references two opposites that are all inclusive. In other words, all creation trembled at the movement of the Lord.

Israel’s failed leadership prior to Deborah resulted in chaos and foreign domination. It was not like the days in which God was the warrior at the front of Israel (vv. 4–5). The roads were abandoned because they were not safe for travel on account of the foreign oppressors and robbers. No one provided protection.

This probably indicates that due to the dangerous times, most people were living in walled cities for protection.

**a mother in Israel.** Since the princes would not lead (implied by v. 2), a woman was raised up to lead Israel. Cf. this “mother in Israel” with the despairing mother of Sisera (v. 28).

verse_quote: When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates.
note: A poetic representation of the cycle of sin and punishment (2:11–19). Idolatry brings suffering to the city.
Later in the song, there is a pointed comparison of those who volunteered to fight and those who for some reason refused (vv. 13–23).

Donkeys were ridden by nobility in the era of the judges.

**you who walk.** The mention of both the rich who ride and the lowly who walk reflects the point that all types of people are to retell the story of Deborah and Barak and, in particular, the work of the Lord.
LORD**.** The Lord’s righteous acts are His intervention and defeat of His people’s enemies. These are His judgments in the earth (cf. Rev. 15:4).
Six commands appear in this verse to emphasize what Deborah and Barak are to do.

–**18** The following tribes and clans took part in the battle at Mount Tabor: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (Gen. 50:23), Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali. Not all Israel participated because it was a regional conflict.
The failure of Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher (v. 17) to participate shows that Israel was not united prior to the battle and remains disunited thereafter.
Obviously the migration of Dan to the north had not yet taken place.
The forces of nature fought on the side of the Lord. The participation of the heavens means that God was intervening, fighting as the divine warrior from heaven.
A city of uncertain location, although it probably lies just north of Mount Tabor.
This section of the song closely parallels the narrative of 4:18–22.
The scene changes from the tent of Jael to the house of Sisera’s mother.
This standard conclusion ties Deborah’s and Barak’s song to ch. 4 (cf. 2:18; 3:11).

Gideon was one of the greatest judges, as evidenced by several facts: (1) his story is the longest in the book; (2) the Lord is more visibly active in his story than in any of the others; (3) the angel of the Lord appeared to him but to no other judge (vv. 11–24); (4) centuries later, Isaiah remembers Gideon’s defeat of Midian as a significant victory (Is. 9:4; 10:26); (5) he is listed first in Samuel’s list of deliverers (“Jerubbaal,” 1 Sam. 12:11); (6) he is paralleled with Moses (6:11–24 note); (7) the people sought to make him king (8:22–23); and (8) he lived like a king (8:26–27, 30, 32). Yet for all this, Gideon was conflicted and failed badly at one point by making a gold ephod that drew him and others into sin (8:27). Gideon is thus the turning point in the downward spiral of the judges. In both his greatness and his deficiency, Gideon points to the need for a better deliverer, a king who will truly keep the covenant—Jesus Christ.

None of the other stories in Judges devotes such attention to the details of the Midianite oppression as this one. Homes, crops, and livestock were subject to the covenant curse (Deut. 28:30–33, 38–42).

Lit. “made small.” The covenant curse is a reversal of God’s promise to Abraham (Gen. 15:5; 22:17; Deut. 28:62; Ps. 107:38, 39).

**cried out.** See 2:18; 3:9.

An anonymous prophet. The prophets constantly remind the people of their covenant obligations. The words of this unnamed prophet (vv. 8–10) are virtually identical to the words of the angel of the Lord in 2:1–3.

**6:8, 9 brought ... delivered ... drove them ... gave you.** In Israel, religious apostasy is always linked to forgetting God’s saving acts and His law. Remembering these saving actions of God and His revelation is the first part of keeping the covenant.

This is the heart of the Gideon narrative. His call is similar to Moses’s call (Ex. 3); he asks the question that is central to the book’s message (v. 13); and his search for faith begins with signs (6:1–8:32 note). The need for a covenant-keeping deliverer like the prophet Moses and the resulting search for one is the focus of Judges.

**6:11 angel of the** LORD **came.** See 2:1; 13:3.

This question is central to Judges. The angel does not answer the question, since the prophet has already answered it (vv. 8–10; Deut. 28:47–52; 29:24–27; 31:17, 18). Some of the psalms ask a similar question (Pss. 44:20; 74:9–11).

LORD**.** The Hebrew text identifies the angel of the Lord with the covenant Lord Himself.

**Go in this might of yours.** See v. 34; 7:2, 7. God will be his strength, though Gideon does not yet know it.
When asked about kingship, Saul uses similar words (1 Sam. 9:21). Gideon’s response is reminiscent of Moses’s question in regard to his call to deliver Israel from Egypt (Ex. 3:11).
See 13:22; Deut. 5:24; Is. 6:5; 1 Tim. 6:16. Again, this is reminiscent of Moses’s relationship with God (Deut. 34:10).

This episode in Gideon’s life reveals how he comes to be known as Jerubbaal. His father’s idolatry is tragic in light of what Gideon says about “our fathers” in v. 13.

**6:25, 26 pull down the altar.** See Deut. 12:3.

**6:26 due order.** That is, according to the prescriptions of the Book of the Covenant (Ex. 20:24–25).
Gideon’s struggle to believe is seen in his seeking of signs (v. 17), which the Lord does not refuse to give him (cf. Luke 1:18–20).
Even though the Spirit has come upon him, Gideon still struggles to trust the Lord.

The drastic reduction of troops demonstrates God’s power to save Israel and brings Him glory. It also challenges Gideon and encourages Israel to trust him.

**7:1 Harod.** Gideon and his men are encamped near this spring, which lies south of the Midianites who are spread out in the Valley of Jezreel.

Israelite laws of warfare allow for certain exemptions from military service (Deut. 20:5–9). One exemption is for the cowardly person, because timidity is infectious and can easily spread to other troops. This is the first test to reduce the size of Gideon’s force.
This second test probably reflects how ready and alert the soldiers are for battle. One who kneels down appears more vulnerable to attack than the one who brings the water to his mouth by his hand.
God provides Gideon with a preview of the victory that he will soon have over the Midianites.

The Hebrews in Gideon’s day divide the night into three watches. Ex. 14:24 and 1 Sam. 11:11 mention the “morning watch.” In the NT period, the Jews separate the night into four watches (see Matt. 14:25). The middle watch signifies the period after the Midianites had gone to sleep.

LORD **and for Gideon.** The Israelites send the Midianites into panic and flight by employing trumpets, jars, and torches, but no swords of Israel are mentioned. Ironically, the swords of Midianite destruction are their own (v. 22).
Israel’s lack of unity is apparent in the difficulties between Gideon, Ephraim, Succoth, and Penuel.
See Is. 10:26.

The conflict here between Ephraim and Gideon is similar to the conflict between Ephraim and Jephthah (see 12:1–6). Gideon belongs to the tribe of Manasseh (6:15). The Ephraimites resent Gideon’s victory because they see themselves as the tribe that should provide leadership for the Israelites.

Gideon has problems with the men of Succoth and Penuel and ultimately punishes both for failing to help him in his pursuit of the Midianite leaders. Many problems during the period of the judges occur because of the infighting among Israelite tribes, clans, and cities.
The text reveals that Gideon’s attack on the Midianites is partly a personal feud because Zebah and Zalmuna, Midianite kings, destroyed his brothers some time earlier.

LORD **will rule.** These verses demonstrate a major antithesis in the book: the people desire a human king to rule over them, yet the Lord is their true king. This conflict finds its climax in 1 Sam. 8. These verses also show Gideon’s inner conflict regarding whether he should be king (v. 31 note).
Though Gideon rejects kingship, he acts like a king (v. 30).

The genuine ephod of the high priest is employed for seeking the Lord’s will (1 Sam. 23:9–11; 30:7, 8).

**whored after it.** Gideon, the greatest of the judges until Samuel, gives the people occasion to sin (2:17 and notes).

**a snare to Gideon and to his family.** Gideon’s father was an idolater (6:25), and now Gideon falls into the same sin.
Gideon names the son of his concubine “Abimelech” (“my father is king”) notwithstanding all Gideon’s claims to the contrary. See vv. 23, 24.

Though not called a judge, Abim­elech is treated as a judge in the outline of the book because he is described in the concentric pattern of the stories about the judges (see Introduction: Literary Features). The Abimelech story demonstrates the disaster wrought by the wrong kind of king. Abimelech is an anti-deliverer, an oppressor of the people, and a breaker of the covenant. His story raises the question of who should be king (9:2, 8–20, 28, 29). In light of this question, it is significant that Abimelech and Saul resemble each other in important ways (9:23 note; 9:54 note). This implies that Saul and Abimelech are the same sort of king.

**8:33 Baal-berith.** Lit. “Baal (lord) of the covenant,” a counterfeit of the God who truly is the Lord of the covenant. See note on 9:4.
Remembering God and His work of salvation is the first step in covenant obedience (2:10 note).

verse_quote: they did not show steadfast love.

note: See note on 8:31.

See notes on v. 46; 8:33. The temple of Baal-berith paid the wages of those who oppressed Israel under Abimelech. Archaeologists have discovered a temple from the era of Joshua and the judges at Shechem that contained an altar and a huge standing stone (Josh. 24:26, 27). The excavators have identified this cultic structure with the temple of Baal-berith or El-berith in Judges 9.
The men were in effect sacrificed to Baal-berith (v. 53 note).
The mount of blessing (Deut. 27:12) was used for a curse. This highlights the reversal theme that permeates the Abimelech story (8:33–9:57 note).
As the product of idolatry (v. 4), Abim­elech’s kingship will be a thorn to Israel (2:3 note).
Jotham’s curse is fulfilled in vv. 45–52.
Both Abimelech and Saul experience an evil spirit come against them as they begin to lose their kingdoms (1 Sam. 16:14).
Gaal is a second “Abimelech,” a lost brother claiming the right to rule by right of his ancestry.
Note the similar speech at v. 2, also delivered in Shechem.

This will ruin it for farming. It also symbolized that the city will be barren and dead from now on (Deut. 29:23). Jer­oboam later rebuilds the city, and it serves as his capital for a short time (1 Kin. 12:25).

Lit. “god of the covenant.” El was the father of the gods in the Canaanite pantheon. This is probably the same temple as the one mentioned at 9:4, which supplied Abimelech money. Now he returns to destroy it.
Abimelech’s words, as he leads his men, resemble his father’s (7:17).
This fulfills Jotham’s curse (v. 20).

Towers are mentioned elsewhere in Judges (8:17; 9:46–49). At the site of Giloh the foundations of a square tower (124 sq. ft.; 11.5 sq. m.) have been found from this period. This discovery indicates that the tower was well built, having been constructed of large, roughly hewn stones; its interior was filled with rubble.

A stone figures prominently in Abimelech’s death, as it did in the murder of all his brothers (9:5 note). This is part of a grinding stone used to reduce wheat into flour; such stones are frequently found in excavations of the period. Abimelech’s death is an example of ironic justice (see v. 56).

verse_quote: Draw your sword and kill me.
note:
Like Saul (1 Sam. 31:4), Abimelech seeks to die proudly. This incident, like the presence of an evil spirit from God (9:23 and note), is a strong point of resemblance between Saul and Abimelech.

**A woman killed him.** He shares this indignity with Sisera (4:9).
God is not highly visible in this narrative (9:23 note), but He brings Abimelech to judgment.

Two judges, Tola and Jair, are introduced with few details. Four other minor judges are described in similar fashion (3:31; 12:8–15).

**10:1 Tola.** Tola is mentioned only here in Scripture.
Like Tola, Jair is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible.
Thirty sons, thirty donkeys, and the control of thirty towns indicate great wealth and power (5:10).

Cf. 1 Sam. 12:11. The list of idols that Israel is following grows, and the internal chaos of Israel becomes more pronounced (10:6; 12:1–7), indicating further decline. Jephthah brings only six years of peace (12:7) instead of peace for a generation (3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28). Finally, Jephthah rashly and sinfully sacrifices his daughter (11:30–40 note).

Many things about Jephthah are reminiscent of Gideon, Abimelech, and Saul. Jephthah, like Gideon, is a “mighty man of valor” (6:12; 11:1). Both men make the Ephraimites angry by not calling them to participate in battle (8:1–3; 12:1–6). Jephthah and Abimelech are both outcast sons, one born to a concubine and the other to a harlot. They gather to themselves bands of adventurers (9:4; 11:3). Both Jephthah and Saul are made leaders in Mizpah (11:11; 1 Sam. 10:17), and both men face Ammonites as their first adversaries (11:12–29; 1 Sam. 11:1–11). Jephthah and Saul each make an unwise vow that threatens their firstborn, and each offers an unlawful sacrifice (11:30–40; 1 Sam. 13:8–14; 14:24–25).

**10:6 gods.** In previous accounts, only the Baals and the Ashtaroth are mentioned (2:11, 13; 3:7). This longer list of gods indicates a downward spiral in Israel’s violations of the covenant. See also vv. 11–12 and note. The peoples mentioned surround Israel on its borders during the era of the judges.

This is the only account in Judges where Israel not only cries out to God but also puts away idols. Elsewhere, they simply cry out to the Lord, and He delivers them (3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:6, 7).

**10:10 forsaken our God and have served the Baals.** The same language is used in their indictment in v. 6.

The list of gods in v. 6 coincides almost identically with the list of oppressing nations. Israel has rejected the God who had saved them and instead has followed the compassionless gods of their oppressors.

verse_quote: cry out to the gods whom you have chosen.
note: See Deut. 32:37, 38. The same taunt is made in Jer. 2:28; 11:12, 13.
The desire to be delivered, rather than to serve the Lord, is Israel’s true motive in repenting.

This is what Gideon was called (6:12).

**son of a prostitute.** Jephthah’s heritage makes him an outcast (v. 2).
Another similarity between Jephthah and Abimelech is their followers (9:4).
LORD **gives them.** By attributing the victory to God, Jephthah shows his faith in God.
LORD **will be witness.** The elders are swearing an oath in order to confirm a covenant.

verse_quote: Jephthah spoke all his words before the
note: LORD **at Mizpah.** The covenant is confirmed before the Lord in Mizpah. Years later, the people make Saul king, also before the Lord, at Mizpah (1 Sam. 10:17).

For the historical background to this conflict, see Num. 20:14–21; 21:10–35; Deut. 2:16–3:11. At the time of Jephthah, the Ammonites hope to extend their territory into what once was their land but has now been Israel’s for three hundred years. Jephthah counters Ammonite demands by rehearsing this history and showing that the Israelites took no more than what the God of Israel gave them and, having been instructed by Him (Deut. 2:18, 19), the Israelites did not take anything from Ammon.

**11:12 king of the Ammonites.** Like Saul later, Jephthah’s first adversaries are the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:1–11). Gilead is the region threatened in Saul’s story as well.

LORD**, the God of Israel.** Warfare in the ancient world was viewed as a battle between the gods of the opposing forces. Israel’s victory over Ammon in the days of Moses was the work of the God of Israel, and no one could dispute the result (v. 24). See v. 21.

LORD**, the Judge, decide this day.** See vv. 21, 23. Jephthah declares that God is the judge over all peoples and gods. Here the word is used in a legal sense, as in handing down a decision, although God will ultimately be a deliverer as well (vv. 32, 33). Judges affirms that God is the true king (8:23) and judge who alone can solve Israel’s woes.
LORD**.** See 3:10 and note. Because the king of Ammon rejected Jephthah’s plea for peace, Jephthah is likely traveling through Gilead and Manasseh to raise an army (see v. 32).

Jephthah defeats the Ammonites, but in the process sins greatly when he makes a rash vow to the Lord and sacrifices his daughter as a burnt offering. God is not to be worshiped in the way the pagans worship their gods, namely, by human sacrifice (Deut. 12:31; 18:10; Ps. 106:37, 38). Although he is a deliverer who has given evidence of his faith, Jephthah does not show the people how to keep the covenant (vv. 10, 11, 21, 23, 27). Like Jephthah, Saul also makes a rash vow that turns out to be a threat to his child (1 Sam. 14:24–45).

A sacrifice that is totally consumed by fire (Lev. 1) or what the Septuagint calls a “holocaust.” It may be that Jephthah expects an animal to come out of the house to meet him. At this time, animals roam freely in the courtyards of houses. Excavations at Megiddo from this period have revealed houses that were two-storied, three-sided complexes in which families probably lived in the second floor.

The sign of mourning over death (cf. Job 1:20).

**opened my mouth.** Vows are sacred (Deut. 23:21–23), and they are to be kept (Num. 30:2). Jeph­thah refuses to retract his vow even though it was an unlawful oath according to the prohibition of human sacrifice in Israel.

verse_quote: do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth.
note: That is, “offer me as a sacrifice” (vv. 30, 31).
This probably means to lament that she will never marry or have children (vv. 38, 39).

Lit. “he did to her his vow which he vowed.” Jephthah sacrifices his daughter as a burnt offering. It is observed that she is a virgin, but this is not the content of the vow. Human sacrifice is sin, an imitation of pagan practice (11:30–40 note; Deut. 12:31; Ps. 106:38).

**11:39–40** This ritual is never mentioned again in the OT. Perhaps it was a mere regional activity that died out after the time of the judges.

Following immediately after the sacrifice of his daughter (11:30–40), this story implies that Jephthah’s struggle with Ephraim and his abbreviated judgeship (v. 7) are God’s judgment on him for making the sacrifice. Ps. 78 (esp. vv. 9–11, 67) reflects on Ephraim’s failure to fight and explains God’s rejection of Ephraim as the ruling tribe in Israel. David from the tribe of Judah is chosen by God to lead Israel (Ps. 78:68–72).

**12:1 men of Ephraim.** Like Gideon, Jephthah has trouble with Ephraim (8:1–5); unlike with Gideon, this trouble leads to civil war. Unity is sorely lacking in Israel, and the Ephraimites grumble against Jephthah because they view him as usurping their position as the leaders of Israel. On this occasion their failure to lead responsibly results in their punishment.

**Why.** See 8:1 for an almost identical question put to Gideon.

verse_quote: the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh.
note: The Gileadites are descended from Joseph, as are the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.
Gilead is on the east side of the Jordan, Ephraim on the west. This seizing contrasts with that in 3:28 (see Introduction: Literary Features).

The Ephraimites can be recognized by the way certain words are pronounced in their dialect. The word is fairly uncommon in the Hebrew Bible, and it likely means “a flowing stream,” “an ear of grain,” or “a bunch of twigs.” Whatever the meaning, it is a rare word used to trap an Ephraimite, who has difficulty pronouncing it.

Previous judges led for forty or eighty years, and peace lasted a generation or two. Jephthah’s abbreviated rule, the increased number of gods being worshiped, and the civil war with Ephraim contribute to a picture of Israel’s downward spiral.

Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon are briefly mentioned (10:1–5 note). Nothing more is known about them. They bring the total of judges mentioned in the book to twelve. The descriptions of Ibzan and Abdon in particular demonstrate that they are men of means and power.

Samson’s story is the last in the cycle of the judges. A Nazirite from the womb, his birth is a supernatural gift to barren parents. As happened with the great judge Gideon, the Angel of the Lord appears at his calling, but unlike any other judge, he is called from the womb. He also experiences the Spirit coming upon him more than any other judge (13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). Of all the judges, Samson is perhaps the most complex. Having taken the Nazirite vow (13:4, 5, 7, 14; 16:17; cf. Num. 6:1–21), he exhibits through his conduct a growing disregard for God’s covenant and his vow. His interest in delivering Israel seems at times to be overshadowed by his pursuit of pleasure and personal glory. The fanfare of his calling and the circumstances surrounding his birth only heighten the tragedy of his life and emphasize the depths to which Israel has descended. Nevertheless, God raises him up to deliver Israel from the Philistines (v. 5), and He uses even the sins of Samson as an occasion against them (14:4).

Though the Spirit comes upon him repeatedly, this has no apparent impact on his character. Yet the account of the end of his life (16:25–31) reflects a renewal of his faith while a prisoner of his (and God’s) enemies. In spite of his shortcomings, Samson demonstrates genuine faith in the Lord, as is evidenced by the fact that the author of Hebrews lists Samson on the honor roll of faith (Heb. 11:32).

**13:1 the people of Israel again did what was evil.** The usual introductory formula is especially abbreviated (cf. 2:11–19).

**gave them ... Philistines.** See 2:14; 1 Sam. 12:9.

Like Gideon (6:11–24), Samson’s parents do not recognize the Angel of the Lord. They see a miraculous fire and then fear the consequences of having seen the angel. These strong parallels pose the question as to whether Samson might not become as great a judge as Gideon (13:1–16:31 note). Three times the Nazirite requirements are spelled out even before Samson is born (vv. 4–5, 7, 14). This repetition heightens their importance.

**13:2 barren.** Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, Samson’s mother is barren (13:1–16:31 note; see Gen. 16:1; 25:21; 29:31; 1 Sam. 1:2, 5).
For background, see Num. 6:1–21. Normally, the Nazirite vow is taken for a set amount of time and not from birth (13:1–16:31 note).

verse_quote: the appearance of the angel of God.
note: She fails to recognize that it really is the Angel of the Lord (6:22; 13:16).
They repeat Gideon’s hospitality (6:19).
Jacob asks the same question (Gen. 32:29).
The incidents here parallel episodes in Gideon’s life (6:20–22).

verse_quote: the young man grew, and the
note: LORD **blessed him.** Cf. God’s blessing upon Samuel (1 Sam. 2:26; 3:19) and His blessing upon Jesus (Luke 2:52).
LORD **.** See note on 3:10.

Immediately after learning that the Lord is with Samson and that the Spirit has begun to stir in him (13:25), the reader is told that Samson seeks a wife from among the Philistines (14:1–2). In this section, Samson’s prodigious strength, poetic abilities, and intense pride and temper are revealed. The narrative revolves around the pursuit and loss of the Philistine wife and the consequences for both Philistia and Samson. In the course of these events, it is possible that Samson breaks the Nazirite vow by touching a dead thing (14:8, 9) and by drinking wine (v. 10). If so, all that remains is for him to cut his hair. Three times the Spirit of the Lord comes on him, and he kills his enemies. He leads Israel for twenty years (15:20). Based on the accounts of the other judges, the reader expects the narrative to end at this point. However, Samson continues to be distracted by foreign women, and the story concludes with his consequent demise (ch. 16).

**14:1–2** The verbs “went down” and “came up” reflect the geography of the story: the Israelites have settled mainly in the highland areas, and the Phil­istines live in the coastal plain. Thus, Samson goes down to Timnah, which is located at the site of Tel Batash. Excavations there have revealed a thriving Philistine city from the early Iron Age.
Israelites must not marry foreign wives (3:1–6; 14:3; cf. Deut. 7:3–4; 1 Kin. 11:1–6; Ezra 9–10).
**she is right in my eyes.** Samson’s desire to take this woman as his wife illustrates a motif in Judges: “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25).
LORD **.** While Samson’s desire is sinful, God uses it for His own purposes to bring judgment on the Philistines.
LORD **.** See note on 3:10. This event sets up the riddle that Samson will later pose to the wedding guests.

verse_quote: she was right in Samson’s eyes.
note: A leading clause in the text; see v. 3 above.
Part of the Nazirite vow is to avoid even approaching a human corpse (Num. 6:6). Many interpreters consider Samson’s act of touching the lion’s carcass to be a tacit violation of his vow., 9

It is the custom in this era that the father of the groom makes the marriage agreement.

**prepared a feast.** At such a feast wine is usual. As a Nazirite, Samson is forbidden to drink wine (Num. 6:3, 4). Though the text does not say whether Samson actually drinks wine at the feast, this is the second suggestion in this chapter that he may have violated his vow.
Three of the seven days of the feast have now passed.

LORD **.** See note on 3:10.

**Ashkelon.** One of the Philistine pentapolis cities, that is, one of their five capital cities.

**spoil.** Reflects what has been stripped off the dead.
Not a custom; rather, an attempt by an embarrassed father to save face (15:1, 2). Even the Philistines continue to refer to Samson as “the son-in-law of the Timnite” (15:6).

verse_quote: at the time of wheat harvest.
note:
A dry time when fields burn easily (vv. 4–5).

**his wife.** Legally she is Samson’s wife.

**a young goat.** Samson is bringing her a gift.

verse_quote: I gave her to your companion.
note: See 14:20 and note.
Perhaps jackals, which travel in packs, rather than foxes, which are solitary and independent.
It is ironic that the Philistines earlier threatened to burn Samson’s wife and her father’s house, and now Samson burns down their fields (14:15).
See 14:20 and note.
Lit. “from lower leg to upper leg,” that is, a full and devastating blow.

verse_quote: to do to him as he did to us.
note: The Philistines seek ironic justice against Samson.

verse_quote: As they did to me, so I have done to them.
note: Samson himself seeks ironic justice (cf. v. 10).

verse_quote: bound him with two new ropes.

note: LORD**.** See notes on 3:10; 14:6, 19.
See the parallel with Shamgar, son of Anath (3:31).

LORD**.** This is one of only two times that Samson is mentioned as having spoken to the Lord (16:28).

**shall I now die of thirst.** Like the Israelites who experienced miracle upon miracle in the wilderness, Samson complains to God. The parallel is marked by the cry for water and the miraculous manner in which God supplies it (v. 19; Ex. 17:1–7; Num. 20:1–13). Both Israel and Samson complain to God, but God in His mercy and compassion meets their need (cf. Ex. 16).

The typical signal for the end of the story, but not so here (14:1–15:20 note). Unlike all of the earlier judges except Jephthah (12:7), Samson does not lead Israel for a full generation (forty years).

This account contains two parallel stories showing Samson’s desire for women, his prodigious strength, and the efforts the Philistines make to capture him. Samson’s continual covenant breaking is judged by God when he is finally captured by the Philistines and blinded (vv. 21, 22). Delilah’s attempts to snare Samson reveal Samson to be a fool for remaining with her. It is noteworthy that the Spirit of God leaves him only when his hair is cut, not at an earlier point of his covenant breaking. God is patient with Samson until the last sign of his vow is gone, and then God judges him.

**16:1 Gaza ... a prostitute.** A common prostitute, not a temple prostitute, from one of the Philistines’ pentapolis cities. Samson once again breaks the covenant (14:2).
Indicates an incredible feat of strength and endurance because the distance from Gaza to Hebron is approximately forty miles (64 km) and uphill.

verse_quote: made them tight with the pin.
note: Lit. “drove the peg,” the same expression used of Jael’s thrusting a tent peg into Sisera’s temple. The similarity is that both men, Sisera and Samson, are unaware of great danger from the hands of women.

See 13:5.

**If my head is shaved.** Samson seems to have ignored the other aspects of his vow (14:8–10). His true strength is the Spirit of the Lord (v. 20).
LORD **had left him.** The Spirit of the Lord no longer gives him strength (13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). God has been his power, not magic associated with long hair.
Samson is taken to serve in the city from which he earlier stole one of its gates (vv. 1–3).

A god of agriculture and the main deity of the Philistines. His name means “grain,” a fitting name in that the Philistine plain was an excellent area for growing grain. Dagon was once thought to be the fish-god because the common Semitic word for fish is _dag_, but this reconstruction is unlikely.

**Our god has given.** God is the judge who allows oppressors to mistreat His people on account of their sin (v. 20); it is not the power of the gods of the nations that enables them to overcome Israel (2:14, 15).

GOD**.** Samson’s final plea is to avenge the loss of his sight. The writer does not comment on this motive. God in His grace answers the prayer and allows Samson to kill the enemies of Israel (10:10–16; 15:18, 19).

A Philistine temple from the time of the judges that was constructed with two pillars that support the roof of the whole building has been discovered at the site of Tell Qasile. This design and construction are unlike either Canaanite or Israelite temples of the Iron Age.

verse_quote: more than ... he had killed during his life.
note: See note on 13:1–16:31.
See note on 15:20.

This section is a twofold conclusion that focuses on chaos in worship (17:1–18:31) and chaos in morality (19:1–21:25) rising from the apostasy recounted in the body of the book of Judges. The section is held together by a refrain highlighting the anarchy that has resulted from the lack of proper leadership: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25).

**17:1–18:31** This section, recounting the Danite idolatry, is part of the conclusion to Judges. The phrases “In those days there was no king in Israel” (17:6; 18:1) and “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6) are repeated in the last section of the narrative cycles (19:1; 21:25). Without a king, the people lack moral direction from a God-appointed leader.

The story starts abruptly with the return of stolen goods. The mother seems to be unsurprised. No reason is provided for why Micah absconded with the silver. His theft of the silver from his mother implies that he disregards two of the Ten Commandments.

LORD **... to make a carved image and a metal image.** This statement is highly ironic. She uses the covenantal name for the God of Israel, Yahweh. However well intentioned, consecrating the silver in this way violates the second commandment (Ex. 20:4; Deut. 5:8), an indication of the spiritual ignorance of the period.
See 8:27 and note.

See 18:1; 19:1; 21:25. The refrain comments on the ignorance of Micah and his mother that is typical of the time. They make idols in the name of the Lord and appoint their own priest. Not only is there political anarchy in the land, but this story highlights the reality of spiritual anarchy as well.

The Levites have no allotment of land in Israel except for forty-eight Levitical cities distributed among the other tribes. Bethlehem is not a Levitical city, so this Levite is sojourning among the people of Judah.

**Levite.** The Levites’ inheritance is to serve the Lord at His dwelling place, the tabernacle (Deut. 18:1–8; Josh. 13:14, 33; 14:3, 4).
That is, in a religious sense.
That the Levite is “content” with the arrangement shows complete insensitivity to apostasy. An appointed officer of the tabernacle is serving an idol.
The religious corruption in this story is highlighted by Micah’s ordination of a Le­vite to the office of priest.
A foolish statement (v. 3 note; 17:1–18:31 note) that further illustrates the darkened understanding of the time, descending to the level of superstition.

verse_quote: In those days ... in those days.
note:
The repetition (see also 17:6) subtly indicates from the very outset of the narrative that the Danites are doing what is right in their own eyes.

**no king in Israel.** See note on 17:6.

**no inheritance ... had fallen to them.** The Danites have failed to conquer the portion assigned to them (1:34–36). They are in violation of the covenant.
They are imitating their forefathers (Num. 13:2, 12).
That is, the distinctive accent of the young man from the south of Israel (cf. 12:6).
Priests in ancient Israel apparently used an ephod to seek the will of the Lord (8:27 and note).

verse_quote: The journey on which you go is under the eye of the
note: LORD**.** The tragic irony of this story—the Levite ministering to idols; Micah’s absurd confidence (17:13)—cancels the validity of such a benediction uttered by unholy lips.

The region in which this city sits is frontier territory where the inhabitants dwell in unfortified towns and villages, making for great difficulty in trying to repel a Danite attack. This city is renamed Dan, and it becomes infamous when Jeroboam I sets up his golden calf at the site (1 Kin. 12:28–30).

**quiet and unsuspecting.** Their peaceful, defenseless nature is emphasized by repetition (vv. 10, 27, 28).
Unlike the original spies that entered Canaan, these spies bring back a good report. Conquest will be easy because the people are unsuspecting and peaceful (vv. 7, 10).

verse_quote: an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image.
note: This whole list (17:5) is repeated three times in the next six verses (vv. 17, 18, 20) and is twice referred to more generally (vv. 27, 30, 31).

The Danites’ action is a kind of parody of the conquest of the land begun earlier under Joshua. They go in the strength of overwhelming numbers against a single household rather than in the strength of the Lord against a fierce enemy. The armed men are mentioned twice as standing outside the door.

verse_quote: be to us a father and a priest.
note: See note on 17:10.

verse_quote: And the priest’s heart was glad.
note:
He is happy for advancement.

**He took the ephod ... carved image.** The priest is going to lead Dan in false worship as he had Micah’s household.
That is, to protect them from an attack from behind.

verse_quote: How then do you ask me.
note: Micah is a pathetic figure, believing that God will bless so-called obedience in any way that he chooses to offer it (17:13).

See v. 14.

**a people quiet and unsuspecting.** The Israelites were to destroy only the seven proscribed Canaanite nations (Deut. 7:1). To other peoples they were first to offer peace (Deut. 20:10–18). The tribe of Dan does not ask who these people are (Josh. 9:1–27) and may destroy an innocent population. Moreover, this is not the land God allotted them (Josh. 19:47).

verse_quote: set up the carved image for themselves.
note:
An example of what it means for everyone to do what is right in his own eyes in the absence of a king (v. 14; 17:6).

**Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses.** The Levite whom Micah hired (17:10, 13). That apostasy has infected even the lineage of Moses was too much to bear for some scribes. Scribal emendation of this text is commonly found in various manuscripts, and it reads “Jonathan the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh” (see text note).

**until the day.** Since v. 31 specifies that Micah’s idol is set up as long as “the house of God was at Shiloh,” the captivity mentioned here is the time of oppression that will begin with the Philistine victory near Shiloh, when the ark is removed from there (1 Sam. 4:4, 11). The captivity in Babylon occurs much later.

That is, the tabernacle, which is at Shiloh up to the time of Samuel (Josh. 18:1; 1 Sam. 3:21; 4:3) before David’s reign. The ark is taken by Eli’s sons from Shiloh into battle and lost to the Philistines (1 Sam. 4:4–11). After that, the ark is never in Shiloh again.

The situation in Israel has deteriorated so much that some of God’s people behave like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:1–11). Civil war between the tribes is the result. This final story in the conclusion of Judges blames the misery of Israel on the lack of a king (19:1; 21:25; cf. 17:6; 18:1). Benjamin is the tribe that sins. Even more, it is the men of Gibeah, Saul’s hometown, who behave like the people of Sodom. Saul’s action in 1 Sam. 11:6–8 recalls the Levite’s desecration of his concubine (19:29 note). Finally, Judah, the tribe of David, is the Lord’s choice to be the leader against Benjamin (note the similarity of wording between 1:1, 2 and 20:18). The Benjaminites have practically become Canaanites. No one is without fault, however. Each tribe is doing as it sees fit (21:25). The conclusion to be drawn is that a king is needed—a king from Judah and not Benjamin. David, not Saul, will qualify. Yet even David, being only a man, proves unequal to the task, as later developments show (2 Sam. 12:10, 11). The Lord alone, whom the people have rejected (1 Sam. 8:7, 8), can be their true king (8:22, 23).

**19:1 Levite.** This man is from the tribe that serves the Lord as His priests.

**concubine.** In this era, a concubine is usually a slave and has a lower legal status than a wife (8:31; 9:18).
The law demands the stoning of adulterers (Deut. 22:22), but the people are not following the law (17:6; 21:25).
See 1:21 and note.

Ironically, they refuse to lodge with foreigners, only to find that their fellow Israelites are no better than the residents of Sodom (19:1–21:25 note).

**Gibeah.** When Judges was written, Gibeah was well known as the hometown of Saul (19:1–21:25 note).

The story of what happened to the Levite in Gibeah is similar to the story of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:1–13). Gibeah’s sin is like that of the men of Sodom, and the Benjaminites are largely destroyed by the Lord’s permission and assistance (20:18, 28, 35). Saul is from Benjamin, and these events foreshadow his own failure as Israel’s leader.

verse_quote: sat down in the open square.
note: In this manner, the travelers advertise their need for hospitality (vv. 16–20).
It takes another foreigner from another generation to show hospitality.
**LORD.** That is, to the tabernacle in Shiloh (18:31).
See Gen. 19:5.

verse_quote: do not do this vile thing.
note: Whatever else may be said, according to the customs of hospitality, the host cannot contemplate surrendering his guest to violence. In the law, the sexual act contemplated is described as “an abomination” (Lev. 18:22; 20:13).

As Lot offered his daughters to protect his guests (Gen. 19:8), the host offers his daughter to protect the Levite. The author does not comment on the morality of this offer, but the whole story is presented as a final illustration of the evil consequences of forsaking God’s rule and doing what is right in one’s own eyes.
The Levite gives his concubine to the men. There is no mention of the old man’s daughter being given to them.
The Levite displays no concern for the well-being of his concubine. The narrator underlines his callous behavior.
She is dead.

It is often assumed that the Levite divides the concubine into twelve parts and then sends one piece to each tribe to draw attention to Benjamin’s horrific deed in Gibeah. However, the text says that he sends “her” throughout all the land of Israel, that is, her whole body cut into twelve pieces. It is thus to be a symbol to anyone who sees it that Israel is not one entity but is acting as a divided body. The original audience of Judges was well aware of how Saul later cut up oxen into twelve parts in order to summon Israel to fight against the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:6–8).
Refers to the grotesque use of the woman’s body. The downward ethical and spiritual spiral of Israel is accentuated by this statement.

The attack upon the Levite and his concubine results in civil war between all Israel and Benjamin (ch. 19). Repeated references to Israel’s oneness (vv. 1, 2, 8, 11) makes an important point: the Israelites are united for the first time in the book. Although their action is not unjust, it is sad that they finally unite only in order to punish one of their own number (v. 23). Judah is to lead against Benjamin as it had led against the Canaanites (v. 18; 1:1, 2 and notes).

**20:1 from Dan to Beersheba.** A biblical idiom to denote the entirety of Israel.

**assembled as one man.** For the first time Israel is united, but the purpose is to wage war against her brothers.

**to the** LORD **at Mizpah.** See note on 11:11. Saul is later made king at Mizpah.

verse_quote: in the assembly of the people of God.
note: After the repeated cycle of sin, judgment, and deliverance, it is an evidence of God’s mercy that Israel is still called His people.
The Levite omits the details of how the concubine has been offered (19:23, 24).
See vv. 1, 11, and note on 20:1–48. The Israelites take an oath to see this through to the end.
The Israelites do not see the evil that pervaded their community.
See note on 3:15.

The ark of the Lord and the priest with the ephod are at Bethel at this time (v. 27).

**Who shall go up first.** The same language that is used at the beginning of Judges, where the question to be decided is who should lead against the Canaanites (1:1).

**Judah.** The Lord gives the same answer as in 1:2 in a different situation.

LORD**.** See vv. 18, 27, 28; cf. 1 Sam. 28:6.

**our brothers, the people of Benjamin.** The Israelites now add the word “brothers” to their inquiry (v. 18).

verse_quote: struck them with the edge of the sword.
note: The Israelites treat the Benjaminites like the Canaanites (1:8, 17). Moreover, the Benjamin­ites’ end is like that of the inhabitants of Sodom (19:14–20:48 note).

The actions of Israel in this final episode should be interpreted in light of the concluding comment: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 25). The Israelites wonder why this evil has come upon them (vv. 3, 15; 6:13 note). As with Gideon (6:13), no answer is given explicitly. Yet the book’s larger context gives the clear answer: Israel has sinned and continues to sin in horrible ways.

This city is located on the east side of the Jordan River. The inhabitants obviously do not feel threatened by the situation in Benjamin, and thus they do not heed the call to arms. Saul’s first act as king is to defend Jabesh-gilead. Since he was a Benjaminite from Gibeah, Saul may have descended from one of the women taken from Jabesh-gilead (v. 12).
LORD **had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.** God does this to punish the Benjaminites for their sin.

Israel’s degeneracy is now so complete that they even propose and allow the kidnapping of their own women to avoid breaking a rash vow. The nation is indeed acting—unchecked—in accord with its own sinful inclinations (v. 25; cf. 17:6).

Israel’s hope is directed toward a godly human king who will reflect the Lord’s righteous kingship. This hope will be fulfilled temporarily by David, but it finds everlasting fulfillment in David’s greater Son, Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:1–14; Rom. 1:1–4).
